newsitem.title: UK: BoE's George says EMU unwise if criteria not met.
newsitem.headline: BoE's George says EMU unwise if criteria not met.

text.p: Bank of England Governor Eddie George said on Monday that Europe would be foolish to rush headlong into Economic and Monetary Union if the convergence criteria for membership were not properly met.

In a speech prepared for delivery to financiers at a dinner in London's financial centre, George said the dangers of a single currency could not be ignored, and said it would be better not to proceed if genuine convergence were not achieved.
"There are real risks as well as real potential benefits in monetary union," George said.

"It would be foolhardly just to assume that the enterprise, if it is embarked upon, will inevitably bring about the political harmony and economic prosperity across Europe that anyone in their right mind wants to see."

Sounding a cautionary note, George called for serious debate on the issue of a single European currency and said countries wishing to join the euro should ensure the economic convergence criteria laid down in the Maastricht Treaty were properly met.

"It would be a reckless gamble to charge ahead if even those criteria were not met -- sustainably and in substance rather than just in form," he said. "If there are serious doubts ... it would be in no-one's interest to proceed."

Earlier, Britain's conservative Prime Minister John Major and Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke expressed doubts about whether a timely launch of the single currency -- planned for les than 23 months' time -- was realistic.
George said the beauty of the proposed single currency would lie in the certainty of Europe exchange rate stability which would help exporters.
But the risk, he said, lay in a single European monetary policy -- "the single one-size-fits-all interest rate".

With different domestic monetary policy needs apparent in individual Euro-area countries, the danger was that a single monetary policy would not suit all members, George said, citing the current three-and-a-half perentage point discrepancy between key British and German interest rates as a case in point.

"Tensions could arise between the domestic policy needs of different countries -- as a result of different cyclical positions, or different fiscal policies, or as a result of external shocks which affect some member countries more than others, or as a result of structural changes in one member country as against another," George told dinner guests.

If the single currency -- slated to come into being in January 1999 -- did not go ahead, or certain countries remained out of the first wave, George said it would be wrong for governments to leap to take advantage of new-found fiscal and monetary freedom.
"With or without monetary union, within it or outside, it is of overriding importance that we all continue to pursue stability oriented macro-economic policies," he said.

Turning to Britain, which has an opt-out on membership of a single currency, George said there was little reason to believe that either the City -- London's financial centre -- of the country, should be harmed by monetary union, even if Britain remained outside.

"Investment will continue to flow to this country so long as we succeed in maintaining an environment offering attractive returns, and our macro-economic and supply-side policies are a much bigger factor in that than the exchange rate," George said.
He said as long as the City was properly prepared for the euro, it too would continue to flourish as a financial centre.

"We live in a global financial world and the euro is bound to become a widely-used and actively-traded currency internationally. Its liquidity is likely to be a key attraction to domestic and foreign users alike," George said.
"The City of London both contributes to, and thrives upon, liquid markets. And the euro-market, or the euro-euro market if we are an "out', will be no exception."
